lines.text: Grouping events into episodes answers what happened. Now smoother statistics over the numbers themselves, running and moving, instead of just marking where one episode ends.
Read the three lines. A running total needs only a tally. A moving average needs a tally from which old rows leave.
And a median needs something different in kind: the whole ordered set, because no running number can tell you where the middle is.
Start with the shape of the frame, because the cost follows from it. Watch the top row: the highlighted block only ever grows.
That is cheap. Keep the previous total, add the new row, and you are done.
In the bottom row the block slides. It gains a row at the right and loses one at the left.
Now the old row has to be taken back out, which is why moving aggregates need the removable strategy from the window internals topic.
Here is a request you will hear all the time: revenue for the last seven days. The tempting answer is a frame of the last seven rows.
Look at the two lines of dots. Same number of orders, completely different stretches of time.
Is a frame of seven rows a week?
No. It is seven rows, however long that takes.
Rows count positions and have no idea what time it is. On a quiet stretch those seven orders spread over twelve days, and on a busy one they fit in two.
Yes would be right only for exactly one order a day, and sorting the table changes nothing about it. A calendar window has to be measured in time, not in rows.
So measure in time. The range frame with an interval includes every row whose timestamp is within seven days of the current row.
Watch the bracket grow back from the current dot. It stops at a date, not at a count.
That might be one order or a hundred, which is exactly the point.
It needs exactly one ordering column, because it works by subtracting values.

lines.text: Now percentiles. A running total is a single number you can update. A median is not.
Watch the values sort themselves. The middle only exists once the order exists.
That is why percentiles are written differently, with the ordering attached to the aggregate itself. The engine has to sort before it can answer.
Four values: ten, twenty, thirty, forty. Look at the two in the middle.
There are two percentile functions, and they handle an even count differently.
What does the continuous one give for the median?
Twenty five.
It interpolates between the two middle values, the way the textbook median of an even set does.
Twenty is what the discrete one gives, and thirty or thirty five would be neither definition. The continuous answer is a number that is not in your data at all.
Compare the circles. The filled dots are real values, and the outlined ones are what the continuous function returns.
Between ten and forty, the median lands at twenty five, a value nobody recorded. The ninetieth percentile lands at thirty seven.
The discrete one only ever returns a real value: twenty, then forty.
So pick discrete when you need a row you can trace back, and continuous when a smooth estimate is what you want.

lines.text: A dashboard rarely wants one percentile. It wants the median, the ninetieth and the ninety ninth.
Look at the top row. Three separate calls sort the data three times.
Pass an array of fractions instead, and the engine sorts once and reads all three answers from the sorted data.
Two more tools. The first splits rows into buckets as evenly as it can.
Watch ten rows go into four buckets. They cannot divide evenly, so the remainder goes to the first buckets: three, three, two, two.
The second reports, for each row, the fraction of rows at or below it, counting its peers. Together they answer where a row stands in a distribution.
Finally, why exactness has a price. There is no cheap running version of a percentile, because it changes with every value seen.
Compare the two bars. On a hundred million rows, an exact answer on every dashboard refresh means a full sort every time.
Approximate sketches trade a small error for one pass and bounded memory. That trade is real, and it is covered in full in a later chapter.
To sum up. Use a range frame with an interval for calendar windows, and rows only when you really mean positions.
Say whether a percentile is continuous or discrete, and why.
Take several percentiles in one call, and measure the cost of an exact one before you put it on a page that refreshes.
Comparing a row to its own neighbors is one kind of question. Next: comparing a row to the exact value another table held, at that very moment in time.
Two checks. First, one of the two percentile functions never returns a number that is missing from your data.
Which one?
The discrete one.
It returns the first value whose position reaches the fraction, so it is always a real value. The continuous one interpolates.
Second check. Ten rows are dealt into four buckets.
Remember where the leftover rows go.
How big is bucket one?
Three.
Ten does not divide by four, so the two spare rows go to the first two buckets, giving three, three, two, two.
